explanation: The revelation of the Glorious Qur'an began with a command — the word 'Iqra' (Read/Recite) spoken by Angel Jibril (Gabriel) to Prophet Muhammad (SAW) in the Cave of Hira. This is recorded in Surah al-Alaq (Q.96:1): 'Read in the name of your Lord who created.' It was not a parable (A), legislation (C), or declaration (D) — it was a direct, authoritative command initiating the prophetic mission.

When Angel Jibril commanded the Prophet (SAW) to read, Muhammad's response was 'Ma ana biqari' — meaning 'I cannot read.' This reflects the Prophet's state as an unlettered man (al-Ummi) who had not been taught to read or write in the conventional sense. He did not say he was not a scholar (A), not a judge (B), or that he could not preach (D). His response of 'I cannot read' is the historically transmitted account from the authentic hadith literature.

During the first revelation, Angel Jibril embraced the Prophet (SAW) and commanded him to read twice — the second time after the Prophet again responded that he could not read. On the third embrace, Jibril recited the opening verses of Surah al-Alaq (Q.96:1–5). The number of times was therefore twice before the actual revelation was delivered. Options A (four), B (three), and D (once) do not match the authentic hadith accounts of the event.

Divine Inspiration (wahy) was employed in the arrangement of the Glorious Qur'an — meaning the order of the Surahs and verses was guided by divine revelation rather than human decision. The Prophet (SAW) himself arranged the Qur'an under divine guidance. The compilation (B) was a human administrative act under Abu Bakr. Standardisation (C) was done under Uthman. Memorisation (D) was a human activity. The arrangement of verses within chapters was directed through divine inspiration.

One of the most cited empirical proofs of the Qur'an's authenticity is its accurate description of the stages of human embryonic development in Surah al-Mu'minun (Q.23:12–14) — describing the nutfa (drop of fluid), alaqa (clinging clot), mudgha (chewed substance), bones, and flesh — which modern embryology has confirmed. This knowledge was unavailable to 7th-century Arabia. Options A, C, and D (sea dredging, nuclear technology, solar technology) are not mentioned in the Qur'an as embryological evidence.

A major distinction between Makkan and Madinan Surahs is that Makkan Surahs are generally short and poetic — filled with vivid imagery, oaths, and rhythmic language addressing basic beliefs (tawhid, resurrection, prophethood). Madinan Surahs are longer, more legislative (containing laws on marriage, divorce, inheritance, war), and address the emerging Muslim community. Option A (historical vs theoretical) is incorrect. Option B (daily rituals vs commerce) oversimplifies. Option C (Makkan addressed only to Makkans) is wrong — they address all mankind.

The standardised copy of the Glorious Qur'an in use today was produced during the caliphate of Uthman ibn Affan (644–656 CE). Uthman appointed a four-man committee led by Zaid ibn Thabit to produce a master copy; multiple copies were made and sent to major Islamic centres, while variant dialects were ordered to be burned. Abu Bakr (A) compiled the first written collection. Umar (B) preserved Abu Bakr's copy. Ali (D) was the fourth caliph. Standardisation — producing a single authoritative mushaf — was Uthman's achievement.

The copy of the Glorious Qur'an in use today was standardised during the caliphate of Uthman ibn Affan (the third Caliph). Uthman established one authoritative version to prevent disputes over recitation. Abu Bakr (A) compiled the first written mushaf. Umar (B) kept Abu Bakr's mushaf safe and it passed to Hafsa. Ali (D) was the fourth caliph who did not undertake standardisation. Uthman's contribution — creating uniformity across the Muslim world — is one of the most important acts in Islamic textual history.

Surah at-Takathur (Q.102) warns that passionate rivalry in accumulating wealth and status diverts humans from the worship of Allah and remembrance of death. The Surah begins: 'The mutual rivalry for piling up (the good things of this world) diverts you.' This is the central message. Options B (moral obligation) and C (avoiding sin) are too general. Option D (praying five times) is not the specific message of this Surah. The warning against materialism and competitive worldliness is the defining theme of Surah at-Takathur.

Al-Kawthar, mentioned in Surah al-Kawthar (Q.108:1), is a river in Paradise granted to Prophet Muhammad (SAW) by Allah. 'Verily, We have granted you Al-Kawthar (a river in Paradise).' It is described as an exceptionally blessed river whose vessels are more numerous than the stars. It is not a garden (B), light (C), or fruit (D) in paradise. Al-Kawthar is specifically identified in authentic hadith as one of the rivers of Jannah, and it is the source of honour and abundance promised to the Prophet.

Surah al-Fatihah (The Opening) contains three major themes: praise (Alhamdulillahi Rabbil Alamin — praising Allah), prayer (Ihdinas Siratal Mustaqim — supplication for guidance), and pledge (Iyyaka nabudu wa iyyaka nastaeen — pledging worship and seeking help from Allah alone). Option A replaces pledge with sacrifice. Options B and D are very close — option D (praise, pledge and prayer) is the correct ordering as it matches the logical sequence of the Surah: praise God, pledge devotion, then pray for guidance.

The verse 'Peace descending on the righteous throughout the night' is a major theme of Surah al-Qadr (Q.97), which describes the Night of Power (Laylatul Qadr) as a night of peace from sunset until dawn. Surah al-Alaq (B) deals with the first revelation and reading. Surah al-Kawthar (C) is about the river in paradise. Surah al-Falaq (D) is a prayer for protection from evil. The peace and blessings of Laylatul Qadr extending through the night is the defining characteristic of Surah al-Qadr.

A text (matn) of a hadith is rejected if it is against natural phenomenon — i.e., if it contradicts established natural laws or scientific reality in a way that cannot be explained. Scholars of hadith apply this criterion alongside isnad (chain of narrators) verification. Being reported by an Arab (A) is not a criterion for rejection. Being reported twice by the same reporter (C) may cause scrutiny but is not automatic grounds for rejection. Not being reported in Madinah (D) is not a criterion. Contradiction with known natural phenomena is one of several grounds for rejecting a hadith's matn.

On the Day of Judgement (Yawmul Qari'ah), mankind is described as being like moths scattered about — disoriented, confused, and helplessly dispersed. This vivid image comes from Surah al-Qari'ah (Q.101:4): 'It is the Day whereon mankind will be like moths scattered about.' Options A (arranged in rows), B (drinking from hot vessels), and D (wearing iron rods) describe conditions in hell or the afterlife but are not the specific Quranic description of the Day of Judgement found in this Surah.

In Hadith 6 of An-Nawawi's Forty Hadith, the Prophet (SAW) explains that the lawful (halal) is clear and the unlawful (haram) is clear, but between them are ambiguous matters (shubuhaat) — things that are unclear and that many people do not know the ruling on. The Prophet advises avoiding these ambiguous matters to protect one's religion and honour. Options A (things prohibited) and B (things permitted) are already in the clear categories. Option D (lump of flesh) refers to a different part of the same hadith (about the heart), not the answer to this specific aspect.

Muwatta Malik, compiled by Imam Malik ibn Anas, is unique because it contains both ahadith and accounts of the established practices (amal) of the people of Madinah — reflecting the living Sunnah as practiced in the Prophet's city. Sahih Bukhari (A) and Sahih Muslim (B) focus solely on authenticated ahadith. Mukhtasar al-Ahadith (C) is a different text. Imam Malik considered the consensus practice of Madinans as a proof in Islamic law, making the Muwatta more than just a hadith collection.

Hadith 4 of An-Nawawi's collection addresses the complete nature of man's creation — describing how each person is assembled in the mother's womb: forty days as a drop (nutfa), forty days as a clot (alaqa), forty days as a morsel (mudgha), then the angel is sent to blow in the soul and record four decrees (provision, lifespan, deeds, and whether the person will be happy or miserable). Options B, C, and D (sun's movement, creation of the earth, seas) are not the subjects of Hadith 4.

In Q.17:27, Allah states: 'Verily the spendthrifts are brothers of the Shaytan (Devil).' The extravagant are thus likened to the associates of Satan. This is a serious condemnation of wasteful spending. Option A (pious people) is the opposite. Option B (pharaoh) is not mentioned in this verse. The Quranic text clearly identifies Satan as the companion of those who squander, warning Muslims against extravagance and wasteful consumption as forms of spiritual corruption linked to the influence of evil.

In Hadith 9 of An-Nawawi, the Prophet (SAW) says: 'Indeed the people before you were destroyed by asking a lot of unnecessary questions and disagreeing with their prophets.' This refers to the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab — Jews and Christians) whose excessive questioning and disputes with their prophets led to their downfall. The Quraysh (B) were pagan Arabs. The People of Madinah (C) were the Ansar. Arabs (D) is too broad. The lesson is to avoid over-questioning and comply with divine commands without excessive debate.

Among the six major compilers of hadith (the Kutub al-Sittah), Imam al-Tirmidhi (Abu Isa Muhammad al-Tirmidhi) wept so much out of fear of Allah that he went blind before his death. His collection, the Jami' al-Tirmidhi, is noted for including assessments of hadith reliability. Nasa'i (A) was known for his strictness in accepting narrators. Abu Da'ud (B) focused on legal ahadith. Ibn Maja (C) compiled the last of the six major collections. Tirmidhi's blindness from excessive weeping is a noted biographical fact in hadith scholarship.

Islam discourages begging by promoting the dignity of labour — the principle that honest work, no matter how humble, is honourable and preferred over asking others. The Prophet (SAW) said it is better for a person to take a rope and gather firewood than to beg. Collective bargaining (A) and labour associations (B) are modern trade concepts. Trade bargaining (C) is a commercial activity. The dignity of labour (izzat al-amal) — the value Islam places on self-sufficiency through work — is the Islamic economic principle that makes begging discouraged.

The verse 'Allah begets not, nor is He begotten' (Q.112:3) from Surah al-Ikhlas is a direct refutation of the Christian doctrine of the Trinity, which holds that Jesus is the Son of God and part of a triune God. This verse categorically denies the concept of divine offspring or divine origin from another being. Hero-praising (A), ancestor worship (C), and idol worship (D) are wrong because the specific target of this verse is the attribution of a son or father to Allah — the core of Trinitarian theology that Islam rejects.

When a Muslim needs to make an important decision, Islam prescribes Istikhārah — a prayer of seeking guidance from Allah, asking Him to facilitate what is good and avert what is harmful. Du'ā (A) is general supplication. Da'awah (B) means calling others to Islam. Istikāma (C) is not a standard Islamic term for this practice. Istikhārah (D) involves performing two rak'ahs of voluntary prayer and reciting the specific Istikhārah du'ā, after which the believer proceeds with confidence that Allah will guide them to what is best.

Qadr, in the context of the Islamic article of faith (al-Iman bil-Qadr), means destiny or divine decree — the belief that Allah has pre-ordained all things and that nothing happens except by His will and knowledge. This is the sixth article of faith in Islam. Faith (A) is Iman in general. Situation (B) and circumstance (C) are incomplete translations that miss the theological significance. Belief in Qadar — that Allah knows, has recorded, wills, and creates all things — is a foundational Islamic belief distinguishing Islamic theology from secular fatalism.

The obligatory (fard) steps of wudu (ablution) are: intention (niyyah), washing the face, washing both hands up to the elbows, wiping part of the head (masah), and washing the feet up to the ankles. Therefore, washing the feet is among the obligatory steps. Rinsing the mouth (A) is sunnah (recommended), not obligatory. Wiping the two ears (B) is sunnah. Silence during ablution (D) is not a required condition. The four obligatory acts are derived from Q.5:6 and confirmed by prophetic practice.

According to authentic hadith, the Prophet (SAW) said that after the obligatory pillars of Islam (salat, zakat, fasting, hajj), the best ibadah (act of worship) is to make a fellow Muslim happy. This emphasises the social and communal dimension of Islamic piety. Praying nawafils (A) is virtuous but secondary to this. Marrying a pious woman (B) is recommended but not cited as the best act after the pillars. Dhikr (D) is highly praised but the specific hadith the question references identifies bringing joy to a fellow believer as the best voluntary act.

Among the Sunnah (recommended) steps of ablution are: wiping the two ears, inhaling and exhaling water through the nose, and wiping the head again from the back of the skull to the front (completing the masah). Supplication at every stage (B) is recommended but less specifically cited as a step. Brushing the teeth with a miswak (C) is sunnah before wudu, not during it. Saying the du'a aloud (D) is not a specific wudu sunnah. The complete masah — including wiping from the nape back over the head — is a recognised sunnah element of ablution.

In a complete rak'ah of salah, there are 6 takbiraat (saying 'Allahu Akbar'): the opening takbir (Takbiratul Ihram), the takbir going into ruku (bowing), the takbir rising from ruku, the takbir going into sujood (prostration), the takbir rising from sujood, and the takbir for the second sujood. This count of 6 per rak'ah is documented in the fiqh books on prophetic prayer. Options A (9), B (8), and C (7) give incorrect higher counts that do not match the standard description of prophetic prayer.

In Q.5:6 (some numbering systems cite Q.5:7), Allah instructs that if you are ill, on a journey, have come from the toilet, or have had sexual contact, and cannot find water, then perform at-tayammum (dry ablution with clean earth). Tayammum — striking the earth with both hands and wiping the face and hands — substitutes for both wudu and ghusl when water is unavailable. Wudu (A) and ghusl (B) require water. Qasr (D) is shortening the prayer during travel. At-tayammum is explicitly the Quranic provision for purification in the absence of water.

If an Imam forgetfully rises to stand when he should remain seated, the congregation alerts him by saying 'Subhānallah' (Glory be to Allah). Men say Subhānallah and women clap their hands. This is the specific prophetic instruction for correcting an Imam's mistake in prayer. Astaghfirullah (A) is used for seeking forgiveness, not correcting prayer mistakes. Allahu Akbar (B) is said during transitions in salah. Subhāna rabbial Azim (D) is said during ruku. The use of Subhānallah as a correction signal is established in authentic hadith.

Fasting is prohibited on the 30th of Sha'aban — the 'doubtful day' (Yawm al-Shakk) — because it may or may not be the first of Ramadan, and fasting voluntarily on a day of doubt out of caution is forbidden. This prevents people from adding to Ramadan out of excessive zeal. The 28th of Sha'aban (A) is not the doubtful day. The 1st and 30th of Ramadan (B, C) are within Ramadan itself. The 30th of Sha'aban is the last day before Ramadan's confirmed start and is the specific 'doubtful day' mentioned in hadith.

Non-pilgrims are encouraged to fast on the Day of Arafat (the 9th of Dhul Hijjah), as the Prophet (SAW) said that fasting on this day expiates the sins of the previous year and the coming year. Pilgrims at Arafat do not fast — their act of standing at Arafat is itself the supreme ibadah. Eid al-Fitr (A) and Eid al-Adha (C) are explicitly forbidden days to fast. Ashura (B) is also recommended for fasting but the question specifically asks about non-pilgrims at the time of Hajj, which points to Arafat.

The Prophet (SAW) said divorce is the most hateful of lawful things to Allah, primarily because it exposes the parties to provocation — mutual accusations, bitterness, and ongoing conflict. While divorce may lead to reconciliation (A), and involves arbitration (D), the reason it is so disliked is the provocation and harm it typically causes to both spouses and their families. Hardship (C) is a consequence but 'provocation' in the sense of the anger and hostility between the parties captures the specific emotional and social harm that makes divorce, while permitted, deeply undesirable.

Islam's permission for a man to marry up to four wives (Q.4:3) is primarily aimed at preventing adultery — ensuring that men who feel unable to remain with one wife have a lawful outlet rather than resorting to illicit relationships. Bearing more children (A) is an incidental possibility. Treating them equally (B) is a condition imposed, not the aim. Reducing unmarried women (C) is a social consequence. The primary Quranic context — revealed after Uhud when many men died leaving widows and orphans — confirms that legalising additional marriages prevents zina (adultery).

Imam Malik ibn Anas (711–795 CE), the founder of the Maliki school of jurisprudence and compiler of the Muwatta, was born and lived most of his life in Madinah. He rarely left the city and considered the living practice of Madinans as a key source of Islamic law. He was not born in Syria (A), Makkah (B), or Egypt (D). His deep attachment to Madinah — the city of the Prophet — informed both his personality and his legal methodology, making the Madinah consensus a source of law in Maliki fiqh.

Allah's pleasure in this world and the Hereafter is obtained through Shari'a — the divine law of Islam encompassing all aspects of life: worship, ethics, transactions, governance, and social relations. Living by the Shari'a is the prescribed path to Allah's approval. Physical exercises (A) are part of maintaining health but are not the means to divine pleasure. Writing the Qur'an on a slate (B) is a learning tool. Oratory (D) is a skill. The Shari'a, as the complete divine guidance for human life, is the framework through which a Muslim earns Allah's pleasure.

Zakat, as an Islamic economic institution, de-emphasises poverty — it is designed to redistribute wealth from the wealthy to the poor, thereby reducing poverty in society. One of its eight designated categories of recipients (Q.9:60) is the poor (fuqara) and needy (masakin). Accumulation of wealth (A) is addressed by the prohibition on hoarding but is not what zakat specifically 'de-emphasises.' Helping others (C) is what zakat encourages, not de-emphasises. Employment (D) is promoted by Islamic economics but not through zakat specifically. Reducing poverty is the core economic purpose of zakat.

Lending money with interest in Islam is called riba — literally meaning 'increase' or 'excess.' Riba is explicitly prohibited in the Qur'an (Q.2:275–279) as a grave sin. Sadaqah (A) is voluntary charity. Kharaj (C) is a land tax on non-Muslim agricultural land. Jizyah (D) is a poll tax on non-Muslims under Islamic governance. Riba covers any predetermined, unjust increase charged on a loan — the core basis of conventional banking that Islamic finance seeks to replace with profit-sharing (mudarabah) and trade-based (murabaha) alternatives.

The core of Prophet Muhammad's (SAW) da'awah (call) in Makkah was the unity of Allah (tawhid) — calling people away from polytheism and idol worship to the worship of One God alone. All Makkan Surahs emphasise tawhid, the resurrection, and the Day of Judgement. Business transactions (B), divine punishment (C), and brotherhood (D) were important themes but secondary to the central message of monotheism. The Makkans' primary objection was to this declaration against their 360 idols, confirming that tawhid was the central focus of the Makkan da'awah.

Q.3:26 — 'O Allah! Lord of Power, You give power to whom You will and strip power from whom You will' — describes Allah's political authority as sovereign (al-Mulk). Allah's power is absolute and unconditional; no ruler or government holds authority except by Allah's permission and will. Complex (A) misses the theological meaning. Liberal (B) is a political ideology unrelated to this verse. Severe (C) is incorrect as the verse emphasises divine sovereignty, not harshness. Sovereignty captures the absolute, unchallengeable, supreme nature of Allah's dominion over all political power.

The Battle of Badr was fought in 624 CE (Common Era), which corresponds to the 2nd year after the Hijrah (2 AH). The notation '624 A.H.' in the option text is technically incorrect — A.H. (Anno Hegirae) is the Islamic calendar; in AH years, Badr was in 2 AH. In the Common Era calendar, it was 624 CE. Options C (625 CE) and D (632 CE — the year of the Prophet's death) are wrong. The Battle of Badr was the Muslims' first major military victory, fought on 17 Ramadan, with 313 Muslims defeating approximately 1,000 Qurayshi fighters.

The pre-Islamic Arabs (Jahiliyya period) worshipped idols primarily because they believed the idols would intercede for them before Allah. They acknowledged Allah as the supreme creator (Q.29:61) but worshipped lesser deities as intermediaries. They were not ignorant of God's existence (A) — they knew of Allah. There were no prophets among them at that time (B). Option D (revealed Books existed) is irrelevant to their local idol worship. The belief that idols and saints could mediate between humans and Allah was the theological error Islam came to correct.

Amr ibn al-As (Amr b. As) was the companion who led the Muslim armies into Egypt (639–641 CE), introducing Islam to North Africa. He conquered Egypt from the Byzantine Empire and established Fustat (near modern Cairo) as a base for further Islamic expansion westward across North Africa. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari (B) was associated with Iraq and mediation in the First Fitna. Ibn Ishaq (C) was a biographer of the Prophet, not a conqueror. Ibn Suleiman (D) is not associated with this role. Amr ibn al-As remains the key historical figure in bringing Islam to Egypt and North Africa.

The similarity between the Jihad of Usman dan Fodio and the Prophet's Hijrah in 622 CE was that both were inspired by Allah — both were religious movements responding to divine guidance, persecution, and a call to establish a community governed by Islamic principles. Both were preceded by a period of preaching, followed by a deliberate migration or departure in response to oppression. The strength of followers (A) was different in scale. Display of bid'ah (C) is the opposite — both opposed innovation. Envy of non-believers (D) is not a similarity of theological significance.

The outcome of the Prophet's visit to Cave Hira was the beginning of the revelation of the Glorious Qur'an. When the Prophet (SAW) was 40 years old and had withdrawn to the cave for meditation (tahannuth), Angel Jibril appeared and commanded him to read, delivering the first verses of Surah al-Alaq (Q.96:1–5). Compilation of the Qur'an (A) came much later. A chieftaincy title (C) is historically incorrect. His resolve to migrate (D) came years later after sustained persecution. The Cave of Hira visit marks the beginning of prophethood and Quranic revelation.

The outcome of the Prophet's visit to Cave Hira was the revelation of the Glorious Qur'an — the first verses of Surah al-Alaq were revealed there by Angel Jibril when the Prophet was 40 years old. Compilation of the Qur'an (A) was a later process under Abu Bakr. A chieftaincy award (C) never occurred. His resolve to migrate (D) came years later. The Cave of Hira (also called Jabal Nur) was the location of the beginning of prophetic revelation, marking the start of Muhammad's mission as the final Prophet.

One of the most important aspects of the first revelation (Surah al-Alaq, Q.96:1–5) is its emphasis on the dissemination of knowledge — the command to 'Read/Recite in the name of your Lord who created' established learning and literacy as a divine imperative for Muslims. The Surah continues: 'Who taught by the pen. Taught man what he knew not.' Description of Arabia (A) is not part of the first revelation. Explanation of existing knowledge (C) and steps of acquiring knowledge (D) are too narrow. The first revelation inaugurated an intellectual and educational mission.

Q.15:9 — 'Verily We have sent down the Reminder (al-Qur'an) and We will certainly preserve it' — is the divine promise of the preservation of the Glorious Qur'an. This verse is the theological basis for the belief that the Qur'an has been and will continue to be protected from corruption. Standardisation (A) is a human administrative act. Compilation (C) was done by companions. Arrangement (D) was done under divine inspiration. Allah's own guarantee of preservation — fulfilled through memorisation, writing, and scholarly transmission — is what this verse affirms.

The wisdom behind the piecemeal (gradual) revelation of the Qur'an over 23 years was the gradual spiritual and moral development of Muslims. Revealing laws incrementally — for example, alcohol prohibition in stages — allowed the community to adapt and internalise each command before new obligations were introduced. This also helped the Prophet to respond to specific events and questions. Compilation (A) and standardisation (B) are administrative acts. Preservation (C) was achieved through both gradual and written means. Gradual revelation was pedagogically and spiritually designed to build a transformed Muslim community.

The Battle of Yamamah (633 CE), fought against the apostates (Ridda Wars) under Abu Bakr, resulted in the deaths of many Huffaz (Qur'an memorisers). Umar ibn al-Khattab feared that more Huffaz would die in future battles and the Qur'an might be lost, and urged Abu Bakr to compile it. This battle was thus the immediate catalyst for the first formal compilation. Khandaq (A) was a defensive battle during the Prophet's lifetime. Uhud (B) was also during the Prophet's life. Tabuk (C) was an expedition, not the trigger. Yamamah's casualties among memorisers prompted the compilation.

A characteristic common to Makkan Surahs (those revealed before the Hijrah) is that they contain a lot of oaths (qasam) — swearing by the sun, the moon, the dawn, the night, the pen, etc. — to draw attention to powerful truths about monotheism, resurrection, and divine might. Makkan Surahs are generally short (not long as in A). They address all of humanity, not just the People of the Book (B). References to battles (D) are characteristic of Madinan Surahs, which were revealed after the Muslims had engaged in warfare. The use of vivid oaths is a hallmark of Makkan revelation style.

The committee appointed by Caliph Uthman to standardise the Glorious Qur'an consisted of four people: (1) Zaid ibn Thabit, (2) Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, (3) Sa'id ibn al-As, and (4) Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham. These four scholars produced the authoritative Uthmanic codex. The number six (A) and five (B) are incorrect. Three (D) is also wrong. The four-member committee worked from the master copy held by Hafsa (widow of the Prophet) to produce multiple identical copies sent across the Islamic world.

Q.30:2–4 predicted that the Romans, who had been defeated by the Persians, would be victorious again within a few years — a prediction that was fulfilled. This accurate prophecy made before the event occurred is cited as evidence of the authenticity of the Glorious Qur'an, since no human could have made such a precise political-military prediction at the time. Beauty of wording (A), historical nature (B), and simplicity (C) are qualities of the Qur'an but not what this specific fulfilled prophecy demonstrates. The fulfilled prediction is direct evidence of divine authorship.

Tafsir is the detailed explanation and commentary of the Glorious Qur'an — the scholarly discipline of interpreting the meaning of Quranic verses using the Arabic language, other Quranic verses (Qur'an bi'l-Qur'an), authentic hadith, opinions of the Companions, and reason. Scientific application (B) describes a modern approach but not the traditional meaning of tafsir. True reflections (C) describe tadabbur (contemplation). Practical application (D) is tazkiyah or amal. Tafsir as classical Islamic scholarship primarily means detailed linguistic and theological commentary to clarify the intended meaning of each verse.

Prophet Muhammad (SAW) did not hand over the Qur'an in a single compiled volume because the revelation did not come in one piece but at intervals over 23 years (610–632 CE). Verses and Surahs were revealed in response to specific events, questions, and circumstances. The arrangement was given by the Prophet under divine guidance, but a complete written compilation was not possible until revelation was complete at his death. Option A (not wanting only Quraysh to inherit it) is not documented. Options C and D misrepresent the situation. The gradual, incremental nature of revelation explains the absence of a single compiled book during the Prophet's lifetime.

The Qur'an is different from other revealed Books because it contains both spiritual, moral, and social values — it is a comprehensive guide covering theology (aqidah), worship (ibadah), ethics (akhlaq), family law, criminal law, economics, governance, and international relations. Previous Books like the Torah and Injil addressed their specific communities and time periods. A prayer book only (A) is too narrow. Option B (helping barren women) is not a stated function. Protection only (D) is incorrect. The Qur'an's comprehensive and universal scope covering all dimensions of human life distinguishes it from earlier scriptures.

The only Surah that must be recited in every rak'ah of every obligatory prayer is Surah al-Fatihah. The Prophet (SAW) said: 'There is no prayer for the one who does not recite the Opening of the Book (al-Fatihah).' Its recitation is a pillar (rukn) of every rak'ah. Surah al-Baqarah (A) is too long for daily recitation. Surah al-Alaq (B) is not required in prayer. Surah al-Ikhlas (D) is recommended but optional. Al-Fatihah's obligatory status in every unit of prayer makes it the most frequently recited portion of the Qur'an by practising Muslims.

In Tajwid, Tafkhim means 'heaviness' or 'thick pronunciation' — applying a fuller, deeper tone when pronouncing certain letters. The letter Ra (ر) is pronounced with tafkhim when it has a dhammah (ُ) or fathah (َ) vowel marker, or is sukoon preceded by a heavy letter. Tarqiq (A) means lightness/thinness — the opposite pronunciation. Tanwin (B) is the double vowel marker (nunation). Tashdid (D) is the shaddah — doubling of a consonant. Tafkhim is the correct rule for the heavy pronunciation of the Ra in this context.

Tajwid (the science of correct Qur'an recitation) is important because it provides the knowledge of correct pronunciation and recitation of the Glorious Qur'an — ensuring that each letter is articulated from its proper point of articulation (makhraj) with its correct characteristic (sifah). Understanding Qur'anic history (A) is a different field (Ulum al-Qur'an). Deeper understanding of meaning (B) is achieved through tafsir. Communicating in Arabic (D) is a language goal. Tajwid specifically safeguards the phonetic integrity of the Qur'an's recitation as it was taught by Angel Jibril to the Prophet.

Surah al-Ma'un (Q.107) discusses the treatment and privilege of the needy — condemning those who rebuff orphans, fail to encourage feeding the poor, are heedless in their prayers, and refuse basic acts of assistance (al-ma'un). The Surah exposes the hypocrisy of those who perform religious rituals without caring for the vulnerable. Givers (A) are praised throughout the Qur'an but not the specific subject here. Travellers (B) and the wealthy (C) are not the focus. The Surah calls attention to the rights and needs of the poor, orphans, and destitute.

The important lesson from Surah al-Kawthar (Q.108) is that Muslims should worship Allah and sacrifice (perform sacrifice/qurbani) — as stated in verse 2: 'Therefore turn in prayer to your Lord and sacrifice to Him only.' The Surah was revealed to comfort the Prophet when enemies mocked him for having no sons, reminding him of Allah's blessings. Fulfilling promises (A) is a general Islamic duty but not this Surah's lesson. Self-protection (B) and accepting calamity (C) are lessons from other parts of the Qur'an. Exclusive devotion through prayer and sacrifice is the command of this Surah.

The verse from Surah al-Lahab (Q.111:2) refers to Abu Lahab — the Prophet's uncle who fiercely opposed Islam — and states that 'No profit to him from all his wealth and gains.' Despite his riches and social standing, his wealth would not save him from divine punishment. Options A, B, and D add words like 'power', 'military', 'property', and 'children' not found in verse 2 specifically. Verse 2 focuses specifically on his wealth (mal) and gains (kasab) being useless to him. Verse 4 addresses his wife.

Hadith 3 of An-Nawawi's Forty Hadith — known as the Hadith of Jibril — shows that Islam is built upon five pillars: the Shahada (testimony of faith), Salat (prayer), Zakat (alms-giving), Sawm (fasting in Ramadan), and Hajj (pilgrimage). When Angel Jibril came in human form and questioned the Prophet, Islam was defined as these five practices. Belief in Allah alone (A) is part of the Shahada but not a complete answer. Fast of Ramadan (C) is one pillar. Articles of faith (D) are the six pillars of Iman, not Islam.

The allegorical (mutashabihaat) and ambiguous verses of the Qur'an are understood through tafsir — the scholarly commentary and explanation of the Qur'an. Tafsir scholars use the Qur'an itself, authentic hadith, Arabic linguistics, and scholarly consensus to clarify difficult passages. Ijtihad (A) is independent legal reasoning used in jurisprudence. Qiyas (B) is analogical reasoning in fiqh. Tadabbur (C) is personal reflection and pondering, not formal interpretation. Tafsir as a disciplined science is the designated tool for resolving ambiguous Quranic passages.

Surah al-Adiyah (Q.100) — meaning 'The Chargers' or 'The Running Horses' — describes horses charging into battle, with the sounds of their hooves and the dust they raise. It is interpreted as a reference to the eagerness and zeal of Muslim warriors striving in the cause of Allah. Al-Qari'ah (A) describes the Day of Judgement. Al-Asr (C) discusses the importance of time and righteous deeds. Al-Humazah (D) condemns slanderers and misers. The dramatic imagery of battle horses in al-Adiyah represents the theme of striving in Allah's path.

What distinguishes Hadith Qudsi from Hadith Nabawi is the wording and the teaching intended: in Hadith Qudsi, the meaning comes from Allah but the wording is expressed by the Prophet (SAW), making it divine in origin but not part of the Qur'an. Hadith Nabawi is the Prophet's own sayings. The place of application (A) and conditions of narration (B) are not the defining difference. Chain reliability (D) applies to both types equally. The divine source of meaning (from Allah) expressed in prophetic words — rather than being part of the Qur'an — is what makes Hadith Qudsi unique.

In Hadith 16 of An-Nawawi's collection, a man asked the Prophet (SAW) for advice, and the Prophet replied 'Do not get angry (la taghdab).' When the man asked repeatedly, the Prophet repeated the same advice many times. This repetition emphasises the central importance of controlling anger in Islamic ethics. Once (A), twice (B), and thrice (C) are all less than what is recorded. The hadith specifically notes the repeated emphasis, indicating that managing anger is among the most important pieces of practical ethical guidance in the prophetic tradition.

Hadith 10 of An-Nawawi teaches that abstinence from forbidden things is a prelude to (condition for) having prayers accepted. The hadith narrates that a man was told about a traveller with dishevelled hair calling upon Allah, yet his food, drink, and clothing were from haram (forbidden) sources — and the question is raised: how can his du'a be answered? This teaches that refraining from haram is prerequisite to having supplications accepted. Option A (only Muslims' prayers accepted) is too narrow. Option B (credible leaders) and D (ladies' behaviour) are unrelated to this hadith.

A distinctive feature of Sahih Bukhari (compiled by Imam Muhammad al-Bukhari, died 870 CE) is that the ahadith are sorted according to chapters (abwab) — thematic chapters that group related ahadith by subject matter, such as purification, prayer, fasting, business, and marriage. By topic (A) and chapters (B) are essentially synonymous here and B is the more precise term. Records (C) and biographies (D) are not how Bukhari is organised. The chapter-based arrangement makes Sahih Bukhari particularly useful as a legal reference work, as scholars can locate hadiths on specific subjects.

Among the six major hadith collections, Abu Dawud and Ibn Maja are the two compilers specifically associated with legal traditions dealing with permissions (halal) and prohibitions (haram) — their Sunan collections focus on fiqh-related ahadith related to Islamic law. Bukhari (B) and Muslim (D) are primarily focused on authenticity (sahih). The question asks for one of the two compilers of legal traditions, and the answer is Ibn Maja (C). Abu Dawud's Sunan al-Kubra contained 'only traditions relating to Ahkam,' and Ibn Maja's Sunan similarly covers legal rulings.

Q.17:23 commands Muslims to honour and obey their parents — not to say a word of disrespect ('uff'), not to rebuke them, and to speak to them with gentleness. Apart from obedience to parents, a key moral lesson is perseverance — maintaining patience and kindness towards parents even when they are old, difficult, or senile. Resilience (A) is similar but less precise in this context. Repentance (B) is a different Islamic virtue. Honesty (D) is important but not the specific lesson highlighted in this verse alongside parental obedience. Patient perseverance in service to parents is the complementary lesson.

Islam as a monotheistic religion expects every faithful follower to serve Allah without associates — to worship Allah alone without partners, intermediaries, or equals (la ilaha illallah). This is the essence of tawhid. Not telling lies (A) is a moral obligation but not the defining expectation of monotheism. Praising the Prophets (C) is required as part of faith but worship is reserved for Allah alone. Performing Salat (D) is a pillar of Islam but an expression of the core expectation of serving Allah exclusively. The call to exclusive, uncompromised monotheistic devotion is Islam's central demand.

Allah admonished the Jews to avoid mixing truth with falsehood in Q.2:42: 'And mix not truth with falsehood, nor conceal the truth while you know (the truth).' This specifically addresses the People of the Book who were concealing or distorting knowledge of the coming of the Prophet. Q.2:285 (A) is about faith in Allah and His messengers. Q.2:177 (B) defines righteousness comprehensively. Q.2:45 (C) advises seeking patience through prayer. Q.2:42 specifically targets intellectual dishonesty — mixing truth with falsehood — as a form of religious deception.

Islam encourages every Muslim to seek a lawful livelihood through the dignity of labour — honest, hard work in any lawful occupation. The Prophet (SAW) said: 'No one eats better food than that which he eats from the work of his own hands.' Equitable distribution of wealth (A) is an economic goal achieved through zakat. Family inheritance (C) is a specific means of acquiring wealth, not a general principle. Shared responsibility (D) is a social concept. The dignity of labour — the sanctification of honest toil — is Islam's direct prescription for how a Muslim should earn.

The Suhuf (Scrolls) were revealed to Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham, PBUH). These were divine scriptures given to Ibrahim, mentioned in Q.87:18–19 and Q.53:36–37. The Suhuf are among the revealed books mentioned in Islamic theology alongside the Tawrah (Moses), Zabur (David), Injil (Jesus), and Qur'an (Muhammad). Prophet Harun/Aaron (A) did not receive a separate scripture. Prophet Ilyas/Elijah (B) is not associated with the Suhuf. The Qur'an (D) was the final and complete revelation given to Muhammad (SAW), not the Suhuf.

Participating in masquerade is considered shirk in Islam because masquerade festivals in African traditional religion involve worshipping ancestral spirits, portraying divine or supernatural beings, and engaging in rituals that attribute power to other than Allah. Dancing (A) is not inherently shirk. Singing religious songs (B) is debated but not classified as shirk. Plastic surgery (C) involves different scholarly opinions but is not shirk. Masquerade — particularly when involving spirit veneration, mystical power attribution, and religious rituals outside of Islam — constitutes associating partners with Allah.

Seeking assistance from fortune tellers (soothsayers, diviners) is forbidden in Islam because it leads to ascribing absolute knowledge and power to a fellow human being — which is a form of shirk (associating partners with Allah). Only Allah has knowledge of the unseen (ghayb). Fortune tellers falsely claim to know hidden matters. Options A (gaining insight) and D (unlawful earnings) describe what fortune-telling does, not why it's Islamically forbidden. Creating animosity (B) is a social harm. The theological reason is the attribution of divine knowledge and power to a created being.

The conditions that make prayer (salat) obligatory on a person include: being Muslim, being sane, and attaining maturity (bulugh) — reaching puberty. Social status (A) is irrelevant — rich and poor, leaders and commoners, all must pray. Reciting with Tajweed (B) is a condition of correct prayer, not an obligation trigger. Following a pious Imam (C) is not required — prayer alone is valid. Maturity (D) is the correct condition: prayer becomes obligatory when a person reaches the age of puberty. Children are encouraged to pray but it becomes a divine obligation at maturity.

Delivering the sermon (khutbah) is an obligation specifically on the Imam when leading Friday prayers (Jumu'ah). The khutbah consists of two parts and replaces two rak'ahs of Zuhr prayer, making it both a communal obligation and part of the Friday prayer's structure. The sermon is not required for all daily prayers (A). Funeral prayers (B) have no sermon. Every prayer on Friday (D) is too broad — the sermon applies only to the Jumu'ah prayer itself. The connection between khutbah and Friday Jumu'ah prayer is established by Qur'an (Q.62:9) and prophetic Sunnah.

The articles of Iman (faith) in Islam are six: belief in (1) Allah, (2) His angels, (3) His revealed Books, (4) His prophets and messengers, (5) the Day of Judgement, and (6) divine decree (qadar) — both good and bad. This is derived from the Hadith of Jibril and numerous Quranic verses. Five (B) refers to the five pillars of Islam (arkan al-Islam), not the articles of Iman. Four (C) and three (D) are insufficient. The six articles of Iman define the belief system of a Muslim and are the basis for understanding Islamic theology (aqidah).

The minimum number of witnesses required for an Islamic marriage (nikah) to be valid is two adult male witnesses. Their presence ensures the public nature of the marriage contract and prevents secret marriages (nikah sirr). Four males (A) and three males (B) exceed the minimum. One male (D) is insufficient. The two-witness requirement is established in hadith and agreed upon by the major schools of jurisprudence. The witnesses must be Muslim, adult, sane, and of good character to validate the nikah according to the majority scholarly opinion.

The supererogatory (voluntary) fast of Ashura is observed on the 10th of al-Muharram, the first month of the Islamic lunar calendar. The Prophet (SAW) said that fasting on Ashura expiates the sins of the previous year. He also recommended fasting on the 9th alongside the 10th to differentiate from Jewish practice. The 8th (A), 9th (B alone), and 11th (D) are not the specific day of Ashura. The 10th of Muharram is the established Sunnah day, with historical significance as the day Moses (Musa) and his people were saved from Pharaoh.

Ayyam al-Tashriq are the three days following Eid al-Adha (11th, 12th, and 13th of Dhul Hijjah) — days of eating and drinking, during which fasting is prohibited. Pilgrims spend these days in Mina, performing the ritual throwing of pebbles (rami al-jamarat). Buying and selling (A) may occur but is not the designation of these days. Visits and caring (B) and singing and dancing (C) are not the prescribed activities. The Prophet (SAW) said: 'The days of Tashriq are days of eating, drinking, and remembrance of Allah' — combining physical enjoyment with dhikr.

The Islamic economic system is aimed at promoting equitable distribution of wealth — ensuring that wealth circulates throughout the community rather than accumulating only among the rich. Instruments like zakat, sadaqah, prohibition of riba, rules of inheritance, and waqf all serve this goal. Controlling world funds (A) is beyond the scope of Islamic economics. Restricting unlawful acquisition (B) is a component, not the primary aim. Restricting men to particular occupations (C) is not an Islamic economic principle. Equitable distribution — preventing the concentration of wealth — is the overarching objective of the Islamic economic framework.

The term Shari'ah literally means 'a path' or 'a way to water' in Arabic — originally referring to the path leading to a watering place in the desert. In Islamic usage, it refers to the divine path prescribed by Allah for human conduct in all aspects of life. Wisdom (B) is hikmah. Passion (C) has no Islamic terminological meaning here. An idea (D) is not what Shari'ah means. The metaphor of a clear path to water — essential for life — captures how Shari'ah is understood as the life-giving, divinely ordained way of living for Muslims.

Among the four major Imams of Islamic jurisprudence, Imam Abu Hanifah (699–767 CE), founder of the Hanafi school, was imprisoned by the Abbasid Caliph al-Mansur for refusing to accept the position of Chief Qadi (judge) and for supporting the Alid revolt. He died in prison in 150 AH at the age of 70. Imam al-Shafi'i (A) faced opposition but was not imprisoned. Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal (C) was imprisoned and flogged for refusing to agree that the Qur'an was created. Imam Malik (D) was flogged but not imprisoned. Abu Hanifah's imprisonment is the specific historical reference here.

Allah commands Muslims to observe and fulfil agreements with non-Muslims as long as the non-Muslims do not violate the terms of the agreement (Q.9:4): 'So fulfil their treaty to the end of their term. Surely Allah loves the righteous.' This principle of treaty obligation (ahd) is fundamental to Islamic international relations. Infringing on women's rights (A), praying five times (B), and changing language (C) are not treaty conditions. The bilateral principle — Muslims must honour agreements unless the other party breaks them — ensures credibility and justice in Muslim dealings with non-Muslim communities.

One of the major economic and social consequences of riba (interest/usury) is that it makes people lazy — creating a class of rentiers who earn money without effort simply by lending, rather than working productively. This parasitic economic behaviour is condemned in Islam. Riba makes some people very wealthy (A) while exploiting others, so 'wealthy' alone is not the consequence Islam specifically criticises. Option D (parasitic) is closely related and accurate, but the JAMB answer of lazy (B) reflects the teaching that riba encourages passivity and dependence on unearned income rather than productive labour.

Mas'uliyyah (accountability) is a principle of Islamic political governance that serves as a mechanism to check misappropriation of public resources. It means that public officials are held accountable for the resources entrusted to them and must answer for how they use them. Indiscipline (A) is addressed through hisbah. Rigging (B) is addressed through shura and transparency. Nepotism (C) is addressed through the merit principle (ahliyyah). Mas'uliyyah specifically focuses on preventing leaders from misusing or embezzling the wealth that belongs to the Muslim community (ummah) — a core principle of Islamic governance.

The first person to recognise signs of prophethood on Muhammad (SAW) was Bahira, a Christian monk. When the young Muhammad accompanied his uncle Abu Talib on a trade caravan to Syria at about age 12, the monk Bahira saw signs on the boy's body (the seal of prophethood between his shoulders) and recognised him as the foretold final prophet. A Jewish Rabbi (B) is not associated with this account. Buddhist Monk (C) is incorrect — Buddhism was not present in that context. Soothsayer (D) is incorrect. Bahira's recognition is one of the early external validations of Muhammad's prophethood.

During the Jahiliyya (pre-Islamic) era, the Ka'aba in Makkah was the venue for the annual poetry competition held at the Ukaz market fair. Poets competed for honour, with winning poems sometimes hung on the Ka'aba walls (the Mu'allaqat). Ukaz (B) was the famous pre-Islamic literary festival where Arabs celebrated oratory and poetry. Ijaz (A) refers to the inimitability of the Qur'an. Manat (C) was one of the three goddess idols. Ushrah (D) is not a recognised festival name. Ukaz was the cultural peak of Jahiliyya Arab literary tradition.

In pre-Islamic Arabia (Jahiliyya), some tribes killed their daughters by burying them alive because daughters did not participate in wars — they could not bring honour through raiding, could not defend the tribe, and were seen as an economic and social liability since they could be captured and dishonour the family. Being the weaker sex (A) is an expression of this patriarchal prejudice but not the specific reason given. Fear of incest (B) is not documented as the reason. Fearing females would outnumber males (C) is not cited. The inability of daughters to contribute to tribal warfare was the primary stated reason.

Mansa Musa I (reigned c. 1312–1337 CE), the famous emperor of the Mali Empire, instituted Friday prayers as a state institution in Mali. His famous pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324–1325 CE, during which he distributed enormous quantities of gold, brought Mali to international attention. Under him, Islamic scholarship and worship were formalized in the empire. Mansa Suleiman (B) was his brother and successor. Mansa Ule (C) was an earlier ruler who first embraced Islam. Mansa Abubakar (D) is associated with the legendary pre-Musa voyage. Mansa Musa's reign marked the peak of Islamic practice in Mali.

The teachings of Usman dan Fodio are remembered today particularly in relation to his opposition to all forms of syncretism — the mixing of Islamic practices with indigenous African traditional religion. His jihad was motivated by the widespread blending of Islam with pagan customs, animism, and innovation (bid'ah) in the Hausa states. Idol worshipping (A) is too narrow. Marrying more than four wives (B) is the opposite of Islamic teaching. Taxing farm produce (D) was an administrative issue. Dan Fodio's central critique was the religious syncretism that had corrupted the practice of Islam in the Hausa-Fulani region.

The members of the Prophet's family who embraced Islam on the first day — Khadijah (his wife), Ali ibn Abi Talib (his young cousin), and Zayd ibn Haritha (his freed slave) — did so on the basis of his truthfulness and uprightness. Having lived closely with him, they knew him as al-Amin (the Trustworthy) and al-Sadiq (the Truthful), and this character was the foundation of their immediate belief. Wealth and influence (B) existed before prophethood but were not the basis for accepting his message. Love (C) and family relation (D) alone do not explain religious conviction.

The verse 'Peace descending on the righteous throughout the night' is from Surah al-Qadr (Q.97:5), which describes the Night of Power (Laylatul Qadr). The verse reads: 'Peace it is, until the emergence of dawn.' Surah al-Alaq (B) contains the first revelation but not this verse. Surah al-Kawthar (C) describes the river of paradise. Surah al-Falaq (D) is a prayer for protection from evil. The distinctive feature of Laylatul Qadr — peace descending throughout the entire night — is the defining characteristic of this Surah.

Surah al-Ma'un (Q.107) is the Surah that condemns making a show in worship (riya). Verse 6 states: 'Those who make show (of their deeds).' The Surah criticises people who pray but are heedless and those who perform acts of worship merely to be seen by others. Suratul Fil (A) describes the defeat of the army of elephants. Surah al-Kafirun (B) addresses religious tolerance. Surah al-Lahab (C) condemns Abu Lahab. Al-Ma'un's condemnation of ostentatious worship makes it specifically relevant to the prohibition of riya (showing off) in Islamic practice.

The revelation of the Qur'an took a period of 23 years — from the first revelation in 610 CE (when the Prophet was 40) until just before his death in 632 CE. The first revelation was in the Cave of Hira, and the last verses are believed to be from Q.5:3 revealed at the Farewell Pilgrimage. Options A (43), B (32), and C (21) are incorrect. The 23-year span of gradual revelation allowed for the progressive establishment of Islamic law, ethics, and doctrine in accordance with the developing needs of the Muslim community.

Tawaf al-Wadaa (also written Tawaful Wadai) means the farewell circumambulation — the final tawaf performed around the Ka'aba before leaving Makkah after completing Hajj. It is the pilgrim's farewell to the Sacred House. Visiting the Prophet's grave (A) is a separate act performed in Madinah. Tawaf al-Ifadah (C) is the obligatory tawaf performed on the 10th of Dhul Hijjah as part of Hajj itself. Visitation to orphans in Makkah (D) is not a Hajj ritual. The farewell tawaf is a wajib (obligatory) act according to the majority of scholars, and missing it requires a dam (sacrifice).

Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim are two of the 99 beautiful names (Asma al-Husna) of Allah. Ar-Rahman means 'The Most Beneficent' or 'The Most Gracious' — denoting Allah's universal mercy extended to all creation. Ar-Rahim means 'The Most Merciful' — denoting Allah's specific, continuous mercy for believers. Living, Everlasting (B) are Al-Hayy and Al-Qayyum. Omnipotent (C) corresponds to Al-Qadir. Wise, All-knowing (D) are Al-Hakim and Al-Alim. These two names appear together in the Basmallah ('Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim') and in Al-Fatihah, emphasising Allah's all-encompassing mercy.

The Talbiyah ('Labbayka Allahumma labbayk...') is recited by pilgrims while moving to Arafat on the 9th of Dhul Hijjah — the Day of Standing (Wuquf), which is the central rite of Hajj. Pilgrims continue reciting the Talbiyah from the moment they enter ihram until they throw the first pebble at Jamarat on Eid day. Mina (A) is where pilgrims go before and after Arafat. Muzdalifah (B) is where they spend the night between Arafat and Mina. The Talbiyah specifically marks the pilgrim's journey to and during Arafat.

Hadith number 16 of An-Nawawi's Forty Hadith enjoins Muslims not to get angry (la taghdab). A man asked the Prophet (SAW) to advise him, and the Prophet repeatedly said 'Do not get angry.' This hadith makes controlling anger a central virtue in Islamic ethics — recognising that anger is the root of many sins and social harms. Drinking alcohol (B), committing adultery (C), and backbiting (D) are prohibited by other texts. Hadith 16 is specifically focused on anger management as the key piece of practical Islamic moral guidance.

The number one pillar of Islam — the foundational first pillar — is the Shahada (testimony of faith), which is itself an expression of Iman (faith): 'I testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His messenger.' Iman is the declaration and conviction that forms the basis of all Islamic practice. Ihsan (B) is the third level of religion (excellence in worship). The first pillar of Islam is Iman expressed through the Shahada, without which no other pillar is valid. It is the entry point into Islam and the foundation of the entire religion.

Khatam al-Nabiyyin (the Seal of the Prophets) is the title given to Prophet Muhammad (SAW), meaning he is the last and final prophet — no prophet will come after him. This is stated in Q.33:40. Ibrahim (A) is revered as a patriarch (Khalilullah, friend of Allah). Isa (Jesus, B) is a prophet and messenger. Musa (Moses, D) received the Torah. Muhammad (SAW) is specifically called Khatam al-Nabiyyin, confirming the finality of his prophethood and the completeness of the Quranic message as the final divine revelation.

At the Battle of Badr (2 AH / 624 CE), the Muslim army numbered 313 men while the Makkan Qurayshi force numbered approximately 1,000. Despite this numerical disadvantage of roughly 3:1, the Muslims won a decisive victory, which was seen as a sign of divine support. Options B (2,000), C (100,000), and D (300) are incorrect for the Qurayshi force. The 313 vs 1,000 comparison is one of the most famous military contrasts in Islamic history, demonstrating that victory comes from Allah rather than numbers.

A pilgrim performing Hajj or Umrah circumambulates (performs Tawaf) around the Ka'aba seven times. Each complete circuit (shawt) starts and ends at the Black Stone (Hajar al-Aswad). Three times (A), six times (B), and eight times (D) are incorrect. The seven circuits of Tawaf are an obligatory act (wajib/rukn) of both Hajj and Umrah, performed in an anticlockwise direction. The number seven in Islamic ritual — also seen in Sai (walking between Safa and Marwa seven times) — has deep symbolic significance in Islamic worship.

Magic (sihr) originates from Shaytan (Satan). In Islamic theology, magic involves seeking the assistance of jinn and devils, who teach sorcerers harmful knowledge in exchange for acts of disbelief. Q.2:102 describes how Harut and Marut taught people magic and warned that it was a trial and that they should not disbelieve. Nas (A) means 'people.' Magic is not from Allah (C) — it is explicitly condemned as kufr. Angels (D) teach divine knowledge, not sorcery. The satanic origin of magic makes it forbidden (haram) in Islam — some scholars consider it an act of shirk (polytheism).

The Holy Book given to Prophet Muhammad (SAW) was the Al-Qur'an — the final and complete revelation from Allah, revealed over 23 years through Angel Jibril. The Injil (A) was revealed to Prophet Isa (Jesus). The Zabur/Zaburah (B) was given to Prophet Dawud (David). The Tawrah (C) was given to Prophet Musa (Moses). The Qur'an is the final scripture, abrogating the previous Books and preserved in its original form, making it unique among divine revelations. Muslims believe it to be the word of Allah verbatim, unlike other scriptures which are believed to have been altered.

The shortest Surah in the Qur'an is Suratul Kawthar (Chapter 108), consisting of only three verses (ayat). It is the briefest Surah in terms of the number of verses. Suratun Nas (A) has 6 verses. Surah al-Ikhlas (C) has 4 verses. Suratul Falaq (D) has 5 verses. Despite its brevity, Surah al-Kawthar carries profound meaning — Allah's gift of abundance (Al-Kawthar), the command to pray and sacrifice, and the declaration that the Prophet's enemies are the ones truly cut off.

Khulafa ar-Rashidun (also spelled Khulafa Ar-Rashidun) means 'the Rightly Guided Caliphs' — the four successors of the Prophet: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Umar ibn al-Khattab, Uthman ibn Affan, and Ali ibn Abi Talib. They are called 'rightly guided' because their caliphates are considered models of Islamic governance. A Muslim community (A) is ummah. A Muslim Ummah (B) is the broader Muslim nation. The faithful (C) is al-mu'minun. The specific title 'Rightly Guided Caliphs' is the translation of Khulafa ar-Rashidun, distinguishing these four leaders as the ideal successors to prophetic governance.

The Prophet Muhammad (SAW) died in 632 CE (Common Era) — corresponding to 11 AH (After Hijrah) — on 12 Rabi al-Awwal, in Madinah, at approximately 63 years of age. He was born in 570 CE. The year 610 CE (B) was when the first revelation began. Options C (519 CE) and D (517 CE) predate the Prophet's birth and are clearly wrong. The year 632 CE marks the end of the prophetic mission and the beginning of the caliphate period, making it one of the most significant dates in Islamic history.

As-Salam is one of the 99 beautiful names (Asma al-Husna) of Allah meaning 'The Source of Peace' or 'The Giver of Peace.' It appears in Q.59:23: 'He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the Sovereign, the Pure, the Perfection (As-Salam)...' Bestowed (A) corresponds to Al-Wahhab. Honoured (B) corresponds to Al-Aziz. Fashion (D) is Al-Musawwir. As-Salam indicates that Allah is free from all defects and imperfections, and is the source of peace and safety for all creation — from whom believers seek inner peace and salvation.

Khadijah's greatest contribution to the life of Prophet Muhammad (SAW) in Makkah was that she gave him moral and financial support. When the Prophet received the first revelation and returned trembling, Khadijah comforted and reassured him. She was the first Muslim. She used her considerable wealth to support the fledgling Muslim community during the years of Makkan persecution. Making him her salesman (A) preceded prophethood. Making him very rich (B) is an oversimplification. Making him king (D) was never her aim. Her moral encouragement and financial backing were what sustained the early Islamic movement.

Taharah (ritual purification) in Shari'ah is observed through Wudu (minor ablution), Tayammum (dry purification with earth), and Istinja/Istijmar (cleansing after using the toilet). Ihram (D) is the state of ritual consecration entered for Hajj or Umrah — it is not a form of purification. It involves wearing specific garments and observing prohibitions. Options A (Wudu), B (Tayammum), and C (Istinja/Istijabar) are all recognised forms of taharah. Ihram is specifically excluded because it is a pilgrimage ritual state, not a purification method.

The four revealed Books mentioned in the Qur'an are: the Injil (given to Prophet Isa/Jesus), the Tawrah (given to Prophet Musa/Moses), the Zabur (given to Prophet Dawud/David), and the Qur'an (given to Prophet Muhammad, SAW). Option A replaces the Qur'an with 'Kitab' (generic word for book). Option B replaces Tawrah with 'Furqan' (another name for the Qur'an). Option C has 'Furqan' instead of the Qur'an. Option D correctly lists all four: Injil, Tawrah, Zaburah, and Qur'an — the complete set of major revealed scriptures in Islamic theology.

Suratul Quraysh is Chapter 106 of the Glorious Qur'an — it addresses the Quraysh tribe of Makkah, reminding them of Allah's blessings (safe travel in winter to Yemen and summer to Syria) and commanding them to worship the Lord of the Ka'aba. Option B (106) is the correct chapter number. Chapter 102 is at-Takathur. Chapter 104 is al-Humazah. Chapter 108 is al-Kawthar. The JAMB data indicates option D (108) as the answer, but the Islamically correct chapter number for Suratul Quraysh is 106. Students should verify with their specific JAMB edition.

A Muslim who hits his foot on a stone and turns back believing it is a bad omen is practicing superstition — attributing misfortune or luck to random events, objects, or signs. This contradicts Islamic belief in Qadar (divine decree) and tawhid. Magic (A) involves attempting to manipulate supernatural forces. Believing in Allah (B) is the opposite of superstition. Witchcraft (D) is active engagement with dark forces. Superstition (C) specifically refers to irrational belief in omens, signs, and bad luck — all of which are prohibited in Islam as forms of thinking that undermine trust in Allah.

In Islamic jurisprudence, stagnant pond water that may have been contaminated or has changed colour, smell, or taste due to impurity is not considered suitable for wudu. Rainwater (A), river water (B), and well water (C) are all considered pure (tahir) and purifying (mutahhir). A pond (D) — especially if stagnant and small — may have become impure (najis) through contamination, making it inappropriate for ablution. The general rule is that water must be pure in origin and free from contaminating impurities to be used for Islamic ritual purification.

The Makkans opposed Prophet Muhammad (SAW) primarily because he preached against idolatry and exploitation. His message of tawhid (monotheism) threatened the economic interests of the Quraysh, who controlled the Ka'aba's idols and derived enormous income from pilgrims. He also condemned the exploitation of the poor, orphans, and slaves — challenging the social hierarchy. Music and dancing (A), drinking and smoking (B), and murder and suicide (C) were not the primary reasons for Makkan opposition. The economic and social power of the Quraysh elite was directly threatened by the Prophet's message.

The place where the Prophet Muhammad (SAW) first began receiving revelations of the Qur'an is Cave Hirah (also known as Ghar Hira or Cave of Hira), located in Jabal Nur ('Mountain of Light') near Makkah. Jabal Nur (A) is the mountain on which the cave is located, not the cave itself. Makkah (B) is the city. Cave Thawr (D) is the cave where the Prophet and Abu Bakr hid during the Hijrah. Cave Hirah is the specific site of the first revelation — where Angel Jibril appeared and commanded 'Iqra' (Read) to begin the prophetic mission.

The first woman to accept Islam was Khadijah bint Khuwaylid (RA) — the Prophet's first wife. She was also the first adult Muslim overall, accepting Islam immediately upon hearing of the first revelation. Aisha (A) became Muslim as a child and later became the Prophet's wife. Aminah (B) was the Prophet's mother who died before Islam was revealed. Ruqayyah (D) was one of the Prophet's daughters. Khadijah's immediate, unconditional faith when the Prophet returned trembling from Cave Hira makes her the first Muslim and the mother of the early Muslim community.

The first man created by Allah was Prophet Adam (AS) — the father of all humanity, created from clay (Q.15:26). He was placed in Jannah (Paradise) with his wife Hawwa (Eve) before being sent to earth. Dawud (David, B), Isa (Jesus, C), and Musa (Moses, D) are all prophets who came much later in human history. Adam's creation is described in multiple Quranic passages (Q.2:30–33, Q.7:11–25, Q.15:26–44), and he is recognised in Islamic theology as the first human being and the first prophet.

Belief in the oneness of Allah (Tawhid) is the cornerstone of Islamic monotheism. Tawhid — declaring that Allah is one, without partners, equals, or associates — is the foundational principle of Islam. The Shahada ('La ilaha illallah') expresses this belief. Brotherhood (A) is ukhuwwah — an important value but not the cornerstone. Politics (B) is addressed by Islam but is not the cornerstone. Socialism (D) is a political-economic ideology. Monotheism (tawhid) in its purest form — the absolute oneness of Allah — is what Islam is built upon, differentiating it from all polytheistic and trinitarian religions.

Forgetfulness is not a quality of the Prophet Muhammad (SAW). The Prophet is described in Islamic theology as being protected from forgetting matters of revelation and religion (Q.87:6–7: 'We shall make you recite and you shall not forget'). His qualities include forgiveness (A), kindness (B), and patience (C) — all well-documented in the Sunnah and Sirah literature. Forgetfulness (D) would undermine the reliability of the prophetic transmission. The doctrine of prophetic protection ('ismah) in matters of revelation and essential religious guidance excludes forgetfulness as a prophetic quality.

The seal of all the prophets (Khatam al-Nabiyyin) is Prophet Muhammad (SAW), as stated in Q.33:40: 'Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but he is the Messenger of Allah and the seal (last) of the Prophets.' Prophet Ayyub (A) is known for patience. Prophet Ibrahim (B) is the father of the Abrahamic faiths. Prophet Yahya (John the Baptist, C) was a prophet but not the seal. Only Muhammad (SAW) carries the title of the final prophet, after whom no new prophet will come, making the Qur'an the final complete revelation for all humanity.

Prophet Muhammad (SAW) was survived to adulthood by only one child — his daughter Fatimah (Fatimoh) al-Zahra (RA). His other daughters (Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum) died during his lifetime. His son Ibrahim (from his concubine Mariyah al-Qibtiyya) died as an infant. Zaynab (A), Ruqayyah (C), and Ibrahim (D) all predeceased him. Fatimah married Ali ibn Abi Talib and was the mother of Hasan and Husayn — making her the link through whom the Prophet's bloodline continued. She died approximately six months after the Prophet.

The migration of Prophet Muhammad (SAW) from Makkah to Madinah in 622 CE is called the Hijrah. This event is so significant that it marks the beginning of the Islamic (Hijri) calendar. Safar (A) is the second month of the Islamic calendar. Hirah (C) refers to the cave. Gar (D) means 'cave' in Arabic. The Hijrah was not merely a physical migration but a turning point in Islamic history — marking the transition from a persecuted minority to an organised community with a state structure, establishing the first Islamic polity in Madinah.

Prophet Muhammad (SAW) lost his mother Aminah bint Wahb at the age of approximately 6 years. She died at Abwa on their return from visiting his father's grave in Yathrib (Madinah). Though the JAMB data indicates age 4 (option B), the predominant scholarly consensus in Islamic biographical sources (Sirah) is that Aminah died when the Prophet was about 6 years old. After her death, the Prophet was cared for by his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib, and later by his uncle Abu Talib. Students should verify the answer against their specific JAMB edition.

A Muslim woman who notices blood after the maximum days of nifas (post-natal bleeding — maximum 40 days according to most scholars) have expired should take her ritual bath (ghusl) and continue in prayers (salat). The blood after the maximum period is classified as istihadah (irregular bleeding/dysfunctional uterine bleeding), not nifas, and does not prevent prayer. She should not abstain from prayer (A). She must take her bath (eliminating B and D as options). Taking the bath and continuing in prayers (C) is the correct Islamic ruling for blood that appears after the maximum nifas period.

The first young person (child/youth) to accept Islam was Ali ibn Abi Talib (RA), the Prophet's young cousin who was living in the Prophet's household. He accepted Islam at approximately 10 years of age on the same day as Khadijah. Umar ibn al-Khattab (B) converted later — in approximately 616 CE. Muawiyah (C) embraced Islam only at the conquest of Makkah in 630 CE. Uthman ibn Affan (D) accepted Islam early but after Ali. Ali's youth at the time of his conversion distinguishes him as the first young person and the third Muslim overall (after Khadijah and Abu Bakr).

The verse 'Fasalli li-rabbika wanhar' (So pray to your Lord and sacrifice) appears in Surah al-Kawthar (Q.108:2). This verse is the second of the three-verse Surah commanding the Prophet to perform prayer (salat) and sacrifice (nahr/udhiyah) exclusively for Allah. It follows the announcement of Allah's gift of Al-Kawthar (verse 1) and precedes the declaration that the Prophet's enemy is the one cut off (verse 3). Surah al-Fatiha (A), Lahab (B), and Nas (D) do not contain this verse.

The religion of the Arabs before the advent of Islam in the 7th century was predominantly idol worshipping (polytheism/paganism). The Ka'aba in Makkah contained 360 idols representing various tribal deities. While there were small communities of Christians (B) and Jews (B) in Arabia, the dominant pre-Islamic Arab religion was polytheistic idol worship — the Jahiliyya tradition. Hinduism (D) was not practiced in Arabia. The Prophet's mission directly targeted this pagan polytheism, calling Arabs from idol worship to pure monotheism (tawhid).

Tayammum is the Islamic purification performed in the absence of water (or when unable to use water due to illness). It involves striking clean earth with both palms and wiping the face and hands. It substitutes for both wudu and ghusl when water is unavailable. Janabah (A) is the state of major ritual impurity (requiring ghusl). Janazah (B) refers to the funeral prayer. Taslim (D) is the salaam ('Assalamu alaykum') said at the end of prayer. Tayammum (C) is specifically the dry purification method — the Islamic solution to waterlessness.

The pre-Islamic period of Arabian history is known as Jahiliyyah — literally meaning 'ignorance' or 'the age of ignorance.' It refers to the era before the Prophet's mission, characterised by polytheism, tribal warfare, infanticide, oppression of the weak, and moral degradation. Sunnat (A) means prophetic practice. Mujahidun (C) means those who strive in the path of Allah. Al-Bait (D) refers to the House (Ka'aba). Jahiliyyah specifically denotes the pre-Islamic period and is contrasted with the knowledge (ilm) and guidance that Islam brought to Arabia.

Ar-Rahman is one of the names/attributes of Allah — it is not one of the names of the Qur'an. The Qur'an itself has many names including Al-Huda (the Guide), Al-Bayyinah (the Clear Evidence), and An-Nur (the Light). Ar-Rahman is a divine name — it describes Allah as the Most Merciful — not a name for the Book. Al-Huda (A), Al-Bayyinah (C), and An-Nur (D) are all documented names for the Qur'an in Islamic scholarship. Ar-Rahman (B) is correctly excluded as it refers to Allah Himself, not to His Book.

Al-Mutamatti' (also called Tamattu') refers to a pilgrim who performs Umrah first during the Hajj season, then exits ihram, and then re-enters ihram to perform Hajj — enjoying (tamatta') the period between Umrah and Hajj. This is one of the three types of Hajj (along with Ifrad and Qiran). Options B, C, and D are not the technical meanings. The Mutamatti' specifically performs Umrah and Hajj separately in the same Hajj season, with a break between them, and is required to sacrifice an animal (hadiy) as part of this form.

The angel in charge of Paradise (Jannah) is Ridwan. He is the guardian of Paradise and welcomes the believers. Mikail (Mikha'il/Michael, A) is the angel responsible for provisions and natural phenomena. Israil (B) is another name for the angel of death (Azrael), though some scholars distinguish them. Israfil (D) is the angel who will blow the trumpet (Sur) on the Day of Judgement. Ridwan (C) is specifically identified in Islamic tradition as the keeper of Jannah, as is Malik as the keeper of Jahannam (Hell).

The early Muslims of Madinah who welcomed and supported the Prophet and the Makkan migrants (Muhajirun) were known as Ansar — meaning 'Helpers' or 'Supporters.' They provided shelter, food, and resources to their Muslim brothers. Siffin (B) was the location of the battle between Ali and Muawiyah. Uhud (C) is the mountain and site of the famous battle. Khandaq (D) is the Trench Battle. The Ansar (A) of Madinah — primarily from the Aws and Khazraj tribes — are celebrated in Islamic history for their selfless support of the early Muslim community.

If a person misses two rak'ahs of Salat al-Maghrib (which has 3 rak'ahs) in congregation, they must make up the two missed rak'ahs after the Imam completes the prayer. At the end of their personal completion, they will sit for at-Tashahud (sitting for tashahhud) three times: once after their first rak'ah (which was the Imam's third), once after their second rak'ah, and once at the end of their third rak'ah. The total number of tashahud sittings is therefore 3 (B). This follows the standard Islamic rulings on catching up missed rak'ahs in congregation.

Zakat is paid once per year (annually). It is calculated on wealth that has been in one's possession for a full lunar year (hawl) and exceeds the nisab (minimum threshold). Unlike voluntary sadaqah which can be given at any time, the obligatory zakat on gold, silver, livestock, trade goods, and agricultural produce is assessed and paid once per year. Twice (B), thrice (C), and four times (D) are incorrect. The annual payment cycle of zakat makes it a systematic and predictable form of wealth redistribution in the Muslim community.

Chapter 112 of the Qur'an is Surah al-Ikhlas (The Sincerity/Purity), which talks about belief in the Unity of Allah (Tawhid). Its four verses state: 'Say: He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor is born. Nor is there any equal to Him.' Life after death (B) is discussed in Surah al-Qiyamah and others. Prophets (C) are discussed throughout the Qur'an. Messengers (D) similarly appear in many chapters. Surah al-Ikhlas is specifically a declaration of pure, uncompromised monotheism — summarising the Islamic concept of Allah in four verses.

Salat al-Subh (Fajr prayer — the dawn prayer) contains 2 obligatory rak'ahs (fard). It is the shortest of the five daily prayers in terms of obligatory units. Salat al-Zuhr and Asr have 4 rak'ahs each. Maghrib has 3. Isha has 4. Subh/Fajr uniquely has only 2 fard rak'ahs, with 2 additional sunnah rak'ahs recommended before it. The 2-rak'ah structure of Fajr is established by the Sunnah and agreed upon by all major schools of jurisprudence.

The number of prophets mentioned by name in the Glorious Qur'an is 25. While Islamic tradition holds that Allah sent 124,000 prophets in total, only 25 are specifically named in the Qur'an — including Adam, Idris, Nuh, Ibrahim, Ismail, Ishaq, Yaqub, Yusuf, Lut, Shu'ayb, Ayyub, Musa, Harun, Dawud, Sulayman, Ilyas, Al-Yasa, Dhul-Kifl, Yunus, Zakariyya, Yahya, Isa, and Muhammad. Options A (55), B (45), and C (35) are all incorrect. The number 25 is the agreed figure from Quranic study.

The primary lesson from Surah al-Kafirun (Q.109) is that there should be no compulsion in religion — 'To you your religion and to me my religion' (Q.109:6) establishes mutual religious respect and the principle that faith cannot be forced. Monotheism (A) is expressed throughout the Qur'an but is not the specific lesson of this Surah. Disobedience to Allah (B) is the opposite of the Surah's intent. 'Say, O unbelievers' (D) is the opening of the Surah, not its lesson. The Surah's core teaching is religious tolerance, non-coercion, and the clear separation of sincere monotheism from polytheism.

The importance of the Hadith lies in the fact that it supplements the Qur'an and serves as the second source of Islamic law. The Hadith provides detailed explanations of Quranic injunctions, demonstrates how to perform prayers, pilgrimage, and other acts of worship, and fills in legal details not specified in the Qur'an. While it also provides reliable biography (B) and was collected by Muslim scholars (C, D), these are secondary benefits. Its function as the second primary source (after the Qur'an) in Islamic jurisprudence — the Sunnah of the Prophet — is its foundational importance.

The Caliph who suggested and ordered the compilation of the Qur'an into a single book form was Umar ibn al-Khattab — it was his persistent urging that convinced Abu Bakr (the first Caliph) to undertake the formal compilation. After the Battle of Yamamah, Umar feared the loss of Quranic knowledge and proposed the compilation to Abu Bakr. Abu Bakr then gave the formal order and the work was carried out by Zaid ibn Thabit. Uthman (C) later standardised the existing copies. The initiative is credited to Umar (B), though the formal authority was Abu Bakr's.
